abstract: The diaphragm, a primary respiratory muscle, contains nearly equal proportions of slow, Type-1 and fast, Type-II muscle fibers. Muscle fiber types - classified based on their shortening velocities and force generation abilities - are largely determined by distinct myosin II isoforms. Mavacamten (MAVA), a small molecule inhibitor of beta-cardiac myosin ATPase, is currently used for the treatment of obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). Notably, beta-myosin heavy chain (beta-MyHC) is not restricted to the ventricular myocardium but is also expressed in slow fibers, raising concerns about off-target effects of therapy used to treat cardiomyopathic conditions. Given that nearly 50 % of the fibers express beta-MyHC in the diaphragm, we hypothesize that Mava may affect diaphragm muscle activity. Using an in vitro motility assay, we investigated the effects of Mava on native myosins isolated from rabbit diaphragm muscle and measured the velocity of actin and regulated thin filaments. Mava caused a dose-dependent decrease in myosin-driven actin filament velocity, with an apparent IC50 of 1350 nM. Importantly, this inhibition was reversible upon drug washout, indicating a non-permanent modulatory effect. To determine the drugs fiber-type specificity, we tested pure slow- and fast-myosin isoforms from the slow-twitch M. soleus and fast-twitch M. psoas. Both isoforms were inhibited by Mava, but slow myosin exhibited nearly 20-fold greater sensitivity than fast myosin, suggesting a potentially stronger impact on slow fibers. Interestingly, the slow myosin isoform showed even higher sensitivity to Mava than beta-cardiac myosin. Further mechanistic analysis distinguished two modes of action: (i) promotion of the OFF state of myosin, likely reducing a pool of active motors interacting with actin filaments, and (ii) modulation of the actomyosin biochemical cycle. Altogether, given the diaphragms reliance on both fiber types for sustained respiratory function, this off-target effect may impair respiratory performance in patients undergoing therapy, underscoring the need for respiratory function monitoring. The studies have direct implications for understanding the modulation of myosin function under physiological and pathophysiological conditions, as well as following pharmacological interventions.
